text: Benjamin Abramowitz, also known as "Ben Hoffman" during the late 1930s and early 1940s, was an American painter, printmaker, and sculptor. First recognized at age 19 as senior artist with the Federal Art Project of the Works Progress Administration (WPA) in New York City, he is among the most respected Washington, D.C., artists of the past century. Born in Brooklyn, New York in 1917 to Russian immigrants, Abramowitz studied life drawing at the Brooklyn Museum School and held his first solo exhibition there at age 16. He attended the National Academy of Design and joined the Work Projects Administration (W.P.A.) in 1936 under the name Ben Hoffman, serving as a teacher, mural assistant, senior printmaker, and painter. The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York holds eleven lithographs from the young artist. In 1941, Abramowitz moved to Washington, D.C., taking on U.S. government graphic assignments and chose Greenbelt as his base for home and studio for more than half a century. During the postwar years, he experienced critical personal and artistic evolution; by day a lithographer, each night he drew and painted with discipline. By his early 30s, he had become a celebrated figure in the growing Washington, D.C.-Baltimore regional art scene, with critics, curators, and collectors actively seeking his work. His art was acquired by major regional collections, including the Baltimore Museum of Art and the Phillips Collection, and the Corcoran Gallery of Art selected his work annually for its biennial exhibitions. By the mid-20th century, he was recognized not only as a painter but also as a teacher and "art coach" throughout the Washington metropolitan area, with among his students the D.C. painter and sculptor Lilian Thomas Burwell. The Ford Foundation sent him nationwide to lecture, conduct seminars, and deliver critiques as an artist-in-residence, while he maintained journals and corresponded regularly with critics, curators, and students. By the 1970s, he shifted from painting to creating wall works and freestanding sculptures and designed four books illustrating the basic principles of the creative experience. Until his mid-80s, when diminishing vision halted his work, he continued creating with the same discipline and vigor as before. His distinguished career has been cited in numerous prestigious biographical volumes, and the National Archives of American Art holds hundreds of papers, letters, and other materials. Walter Hopps, museum director and curator, stated at a memorial service for artist Gene Davis at the National Gallery of Art in 1985 that "the modern art movement in the Washington region started mid-century, and the first was the work of Ben Abramowitz." The prolific and complex achievements of master artist Benjamin Abramowitz in painting, sculpture, works on paper in drawing and watercolor span almost eight decades. Noted for his compelling aesthetic vision, Abramowitz has been hailed by critics, curators, and collectors as one of the most important artists of the 20th century. His vast body of work resists categorization, and despite working outside the geographical spotlight of the New York art world, his recognized mastery has been remarkably overlooked.
